subject: Accounting
title: Journalizing and Posting
description: A quick win: understand Journalizing and Posting.

hook.text: Every transaction gets written twice—once as a debit, once as a credit. That's the journal.

buildup.text: The journal is the chronological diary of all business transactions.

discovery.text: After journalizing, entries are posted to the ledger—organized by account, not by date.

twist.text: A journal shows what happened when. A ledger shows the running total for each account.

climax.text: Together they create a complete, cross-referenced record of every financial move.

punchline.text: Journals record events. Ledgers organize them.

details.summary: Journalizing records transactions as journal entries in chronological order; posting transfers those entries to individual accounts in the general ledger. Together, these steps transform raw transaction data into organized, account-specific records.
details.whyItMatters: Journalizing and posting are the mechanical heart of double-entry bookkeeping. Every financial report—from the income statement to the tax return—traces back to these fundamental steps.
takeaways: Journal entries record the date, accounts affected, debit and credit amounts, and a brief description
Posting transfers journal entry amounts to the appropriate accounts in the general ledger
The general ledger organizes data by account, making it possible to calculate account balances

faq.question: What is the difference between a journal and a ledger?
faq.answer: A journal records transactions in chronological order—like a diary of financial events. A ledger organizes that same information by account—grouping all cash transactions together, all revenue together, etc. The journal shows what happened when; the ledger shows where things stand.

faq.question: Why do journal entries have debits and credits?
faq.answer: Double-entry bookkeeping requires that every transaction affects at least two accounts with equal debits and credits. This ensures the accounting equation stays balanced and creates a self-checking system that catches errors when debits don't equal credits.
